A_target.statement:
Let $A$ be an [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian group]] with [[Definition:Torsion Subgroup|torsion subgroup]] $\map T A$.
Then $A / \map T A$ is [[Definition:Torsion-Free Group|torsion-free]].

B_source.statement:
Let $X$ be the set of elements of an algebraic structure exhibiting a property.
If $X$ is closed under the relevant operations, collapsing $X$ can remove the property from the quotient.

substitutions.the subobject of offending elements: the torsion subgroup, the elements of finite order
substitutions.the quotient: the group modulo its torsion subgroup

derived.an offending element of the quotient: an element whose multiple lies in the torsion subgroup
derived.lifting the offence back: that element itself has finite order, so it was already collapsed

object_map.reformulation: Collapse precisely the elements exhibiting the property, so that any surviving instance lifts back into what was already removed.

validity_conditions: The torsion elements form a subgroup because the group is abelian; for a nonabelian group the elements of finite order need not be closed under multiplication and the construction fails.
If a class has finite order then some multiple of a representative lies in the torsion subgroup, so a further multiple is trivial and the representative was already torsion.
Hence the only torsion class is the identity class, which is exactly torsion freeness of the quotient.
proof_plan:
If $m a = 0$ and $n b = 0$ then $m n \paren {a - b} = n \paren {m a} - m \paren {n b} = 0$, using commutativity.
Hence $\map T A$ is a [[Definition:Subgroup|subgroup]].

Let $a + \map T A$ have finite order $n$.
Then $n a \in \map T A$, so $m \paren {n a} = 0$ for some $m > 0$.
